paragraphs.context: I get many letters telling me how much kids learn from reading Magic Tree House books.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer learns a lot when she writes.
paragraphs.simple: Children write to say they learn a lot from these books. But the writer learns a lot too. She is not an expert, so she must do a lot of research.

paragraphs.context: Working on Dingoes at Dinnertime, I was surprised to discover how little I really knew about the continent of Australia.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She learned about Australia's special animals.
paragraphs.simple: The writer did not know much about Australia. She did not know why some animals live only there, like kangaroos, koalas and emus.

background.note: Australia is a country and also a continent, south-east of Asia. Many of its animals live nowhere else on earth.

paragraphs.context: But after I did my research, I found out the answer.
paragraphs.mainIdea: You will find the answer in the book.
paragraphs.simple: After her research, she knew the answer. Readers will learn it with Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: I hope that reading Dingoes at Dinnertime will be just the beginning of your Australian adventure.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She hopes you will learn more about Australia.
paragraphs.simple: The writer hopes this book will make you want to find out more about Australia by yourself.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the story of the magic tree house began.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house was suddenly in the woods near Jack and Annie's town.

background.note: Frog Creek is the small town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She is a magic librarian from long ago who travels through time and collects books.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic woman in the old stories about King Arthur. In these books she is a kind librarian.
King Arthur is a king in old British stories. He lived in a castle called Camelot.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #17–20, Jack and Annie must be given four special gifts
paragraphs.simple: They must get four gifts to free a dog from magic. They have three gifts: from the Titanic, from the Lakota and from India. Now they go to find the last one.

background.note: The Titanic was a very big ship. It hit an iceberg and sank in 1912. Jack and Annie went there in book 17.
The Lakota are a Native American people of the Great Plains in the USA. Jack and Annie visited them in book 18.

paragraphs.context: Annie sat on the porch steps.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sat outside the front door and looked at the woods. She thinks she hears Teddy.

paragraphs.context: “You’re kidding,” said Jack. But he looked down the street and listened, too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not believe her, but he listens. Far away there is a small bark. Jack smiles.

paragraphs.simple: A drought is a long time with no rain. But at other times the same forest can be covered with water from heavy rain.

background.note: Australia often has droughts. Then the land is very dry and fires start easily.

background.note: A teddy bear is a soft toy bear. The toy is named after the American president Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt.

paragraphs.context: The creature was fast asleep.
paragraphs.simple: The animal was sleeping deeply. It had round ears, a black nose, a furry body and long, curved nails.

paragraphs.context: The koala is actually not a bear at all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A koala is a marsupial, not a bear.
paragraphs.simple: A koala is not really a bear. It is a marsupial, like a kangaroo: the mother carries her babies in a pocket on her stomach.

paragraphs.context: Koalas mostly eat the leaves of gum trees
paragraphs.simple: Koalas eat gum tree leaves. When people cut down the trees, koalas lose their food. Fires are dangerous for koalas too, because they move slowly.

background.note: Wildfires (in Australia often called bushfires) happen often in the hot, dry summer.
Gum trees (eucalyptus trees) are tall Australian trees. Their leaves have a strong smell. Koalas eat almost nothing else.

paragraphs.context: Koalas, like kangaroos, are active at night and sleep during the day
paragraphs.simple: Koalas sleep in the day and move at night. Their name means "no drink", because they get water from leaves.

paragraphs.context: “Speaking of water,” he said, “I’m thirsty.”
paragraphs.simple: Talking about water makes Jack want a drink. Annie and Teddy are thirsty too.

paragraphs.context: She pointed at a bird in a gum tree.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sound comes from a bird.
paragraphs.simple: A brown bird with a big head and long beak looked down and made the sound again.

paragraphs.context: The kookaburra (say KOOK-uh-burr-uh) is the best-known bird of Australia.
paragraphs.simple: The kookaburra is Australia's most famous bird. Its call sounds like a laughing donkey.

background.note: "Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree" is a famous Australian children's song from 1932. Children sing it in many countries.

paragraphs.context: “Kookaburra sits on the old gum tree-ee.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sings the old song about the kookaburra in the gum tree.
paragraphs.tone: Happy and fun. The "-ee" shows how the song is sung.

paragraphs.context: Merry, merry king of the bush is he-ee … ”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The second line of the song.
paragraphs.simple: The song says the kookaburra is the happy king of the wild Australian land.

background.note: In Australia, "the bush" means the wild land outside the towns, with trees and bushes.

paragraphs.context: Annie pointed to a big bluish tan lump lying in a shallow, dusty hole.
paragraphs.simple: In a small dusty hole there was a big blue-brown shape. It was breathing.

paragraphs.context: The lump was an animal lying on its back.
paragraphs.simple: The animal was on its back with its paws on its chest. It had big feet, big ears and a long tail.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, wow! It’s a kangaroo with her baby in her pouch!” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is a kangaroo with a baby.
paragraphs.simple: A small head looked out of the animal's stomach. It was a baby kangaroo in its mother's pouch.

paragraphs.context: Their voices woke the kangaroo.
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo jumped up, looked at them angrily and hit the ground with her foot.

paragraphs.context: The kangaroo eyed Annie curiously.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie and the kangaroo hop together.
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo looked at Annie and hopped toward her. Annie hopped too. It looked like they were dancing.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t believe how graceful the kangaroo was.
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo seemed to fly and then land very softly, like a butterfly.

paragraphs.context: The kangaroo is the most famous of the marsupials.
paragraphs.simple: A baby kangaroo is called a joey. Kangaroos have big feet and can jump very high, even over a school bus.

background.note: "Macropod" comes from Greek words: "macro" (big) and "pod" (foot).

paragraphs.context: “Forget the hopping contest, Annie,” Jack called.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Annie should stop the game, because the kangaroo can hop much better than her.

paragraphs.context: A moment later, three dogs crept silently into the clearing.
paragraphs.simple: Three sand-coloured dogs that looked dangerous came quietly toward the kangaroo.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, the mother kangaroo sprang into the air, away from the dogs.
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo jumped away and the dogs ran after her. Annie shouted at them to stop.

paragraphs.context: As the kangaroo jumped, she turned in midair
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo turned while in the air and jumped this way and that way over rocks. The dogs ran after her, howling.

paragraphs.context: Jack ran after Annie with the book under his arm.
paragraphs.simple: Jack ran over the dry ground past bushes and trees, watching Annie. She suddenly stopped and knelt down.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached Annie. Beside her in the grass was the baby kangaroo.
paragraphs.simple: The baby kangaroo was in the grass, shaking with fear. Annie wonders why the mother left him.

paragraphs.context: The biggest enemy of the kangaroo is the dingo
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the mother left her baby.
paragraphs.simple: When dingoes chase a mother kangaroo, she may throw her baby out of her pouch. Then she can jump faster and lead the dogs away. If she escapes, she comes back for the baby.

background.note: Dingoes are wild dogs that have lived in Australia for thousands of years. They hunt kangaroos and other animals.

paragraphs.context: “Hi, Joey,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie calls the baby Joey, because a baby kangaroo is called a joey. His fur is very soft.

paragraphs.context: The baby kangaroo took a giant leap and dived headfirst into the pack!
paragraphs.simple: Joey jumped head first into Jack's backpack. Only his big feet stuck out. Then he turned over and looked out.

paragraphs.context: “He thinks your pack is a pouch!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie helps Jack wear the pack on his chest, like a pouch. Joey is heavy. Annie says Jack looks like a mother kangaroo.

paragraphs.context: He munched the grass, keeping his big eyes on Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Joey ate the grass and watched Annie all the time. Annie hopes his mother comes back soon.

paragraphs.context: He looked around the dry forest. There was no sign of the mother kangaroo.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not see the mother anywhere. But he saw something else.

paragraphs.context: The wisp of smoke in the sky had turned into a big black cloud.
paragraphs.simple: The thin smoke was now a big black cloud, and the smell of burning wood was stronger.

paragraphs.context: A feeling of dread came over Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack suddenly felt very afraid. Far away, a tree started to burn. It is a big forest fire!
paragraphs.tone: Frightening. The "What if ..." shows Jack is too afraid to finish.

paragraphs.context: “The woods are so dry, everything’s starting to burn!”
paragraphs.simple: The forest is so dry that everything is burning. Jack says they must go and take Joey with them.

paragraphs.context: Just then, the kookaburra flew through the sky, cackling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the animals run from the fire.
paragraphs.simple: The bird flew away and the emus ran very fast. The smoke got thicker and the fire spread quickly.

paragraphs.context: Smoke hid the treetops. Jack’s eyes stung.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They cannot find the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Smoke covered the trees and hurt Jack's eyes. He decides they must just get away from the smoke.

paragraphs.context: But Annie had dashed off in the other direction.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie runs back into the smoke.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs the other way to get something. Jack shouts for her to come back.

paragraphs.context: Jack choked on the smoke.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not breathe well and coughed. The air got hotter. He had to run.

paragraphs.context: He stumbled blindly through the brush.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not see and almost fell many times. He followed Teddy's barking. His pack got heavier.

paragraphs.context: Annie appeared through the haze of the hot smoke.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie comes back with the koala.
paragraphs.simple: Annie came out of the smoke, coughing and crying from the smoke. She was carrying the koala!
paragraphs.tone: Brave and kind: Annie went back to save the koala.

paragraphs.context: Teddy was standing on a ledge. Behind him was the mouth of a cave.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy stood on a narrow flat rock in front of a cave. Then he went inside.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie climbed onto the rock ledge and stepped into the cave.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are safe in the cave.
paragraphs.simple: The air in the cave was cleaner and cooler. It was very dark.

paragraphs.context: She held out her free hand to Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk into the dark cave.
paragraphs.simple: Annie held Jack's hand. Jack touched the wall with his other hand, and they walked into the dark.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, Jack felt something thump against his leg.
paragraphs.simple: Something hit Jack's leg. It was Teddy's happy tail.

paragraphs.context: A white line began to glow in the air.
paragraphs.simple: A glowing line became a big snake, with glowing handprints under it.

paragraphs.context: Despite the glowing painting, the rock felt smooth and cool.
paragraphs.simple: The painting glowed, but the rock was cool and smooth. It almost seemed to breathe. Then they heard wind and a loud boom.

paragraphs.context: “Lightning,” said Annie. “Lightning and thunder!
paragraphs.simple: They saw lightning at the front of the cave. Annie pulled Jack out into heavy rain.

paragraphs.context: Rain fell on Jack’s head and on Joey’s head.
paragraphs.simple: Rain fell on all of them. Annie and Jack drank the rainwater. It was the best water Jack ever had.

paragraphs.context: When Jack looked back at the woods, misty steam was rising
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rain puts out the fire.
paragraphs.simple: Steam rose from the black, burned ground. The heavy rain was stopping the fire.

paragraphs.context: They walked over to the unburned gum tree.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They put the koala back in a tree.
paragraphs.simple: They put the koala in a gum tree that did not burn. Annie told it to go back to sleep.

paragraphs.context: The koala seemed to smile at them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The koala goes back to sleep.
paragraphs.simple: The koala closed its eyes and slept, as if nothing had happened.

paragraphs.context: “It wasn’t just luck,” she said. “It was magic.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks the painting brought the rain.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the glowing hands and snake brought the storm. Jack does not believe it.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, we have to get Joey back to the place where his mom left him,”
paragraphs.simple: The mother kangaroo will look for Joey where she left him. But they do not know where that place is.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie caught up with Teddy. He stood over the Australia book!
paragraphs.simple: Teddy found the book. Jack left it in the place where they found Joey, so this is the right place.

paragraphs.context: The rain turned to a drizzle.
paragraphs.simple: The rain became lighter and lighter. "Turned to" here means "changed into". They waited and waited.

paragraphs.context: Maybe the mother kangaroo had come and left.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid for the mother.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks of bad things: maybe the mother left, or the dingoes caught her, or the fire killed her.

paragraphs.context: It was a squishy sound. It was a squashy sound.
paragraphs.simple: They heard the soft, wet sound of big feet hitting mud. The words "squishy" and "squashy" let you hear the sound.

paragraphs.context: The mother kangaroo bounded out of the trees.
paragraphs.simple: The mother kangaroo jumped out of the trees and landed about 3 metres away. Everyone stopped moving.

paragraphs.context: He leaped again … then again … and dived headfirst into his mother’s pouch!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joey goes back to his mother.
paragraphs.simple: Joey jumped into his mother's pouch head first. Jack and Annie were very happy.

paragraphs.context: The mother kangaroo was gazing down at her joey.
paragraphs.simple: The mother looked at her baby with love, then looked kindly at Jack and Annie, as if to say thank you.

paragraphs.context: The kangaroo gave a little nod.
paragraphs.simple: The kangaroo picked up a small piece of tree bark and gave it to them. It is the gift from a kangaroo!

paragraphs.context: The rain stopped as Jack studied the piece of bark.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bark has the snake picture on it.
paragraphs.simple: The bark had a small painting, just like the snake painting in the cave.

paragraphs.context: The first people of Australia are called “Aborigines”
paragraphs.simple: The first people of Australia have lived there for 40,000 years. In their old stories, a Rainbow Serpent sends rain that gives life.

background.note: Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for at least 40,000 years. Their culture is one of the oldest in the world.
Aboriginal people are the first people of Australia. Today most people say "Aboriginal people" or "Aboriginal Australians".
The Dreamtime (or "the Dreaming") is the time in Aboriginal stories when the land, animals and people were made.

paragraphs.context: Aborigine artists paint the Rainbow Serpent on cave walls or on pieces of bark.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How people honour the Rainbow Serpent.
paragraphs.simple: Artists paint the snake on cave walls or bark. In special events, they put painted handprints on it.

background.note: The Rainbow Serpent is a great snake in many Aboriginal stories. It makes rivers and brings rain and life.

paragraphs.context: “We put our hands on the painting of the Rainbow Serpent,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says their handprints were like a ceremony, so the Rainbow Serpent sent rain to stop the fire.

paragraphs.context: “But it’s not a real creature,” he said. “It’s in Dream time. Not real time.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the snake is only in old stories. (The book writes "Dream time" as two words here, but "Dreamtime" in other places.)

paragraphs.context: A rainbow curved across the blue Australian sky.
paragraphs.simple: A rainbow was in the sky, like the Rainbow Serpent. Jack shivered, even though it was warm.

paragraphs.context: “I told you,” said Annie. “He has a touch of magic.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Teddy has a little bit of magic in him. Teddy seems to smile.

paragraphs.context: Then they all headed through the wet, steamy forest in the direction of the tree house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go back to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They walked through the wet forest toward the tree house. Jack hoped it did not burn.

paragraphs.context: “Over the rainbow!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wishes to go home, and Annie shouts the name of a famous song.

background.note: "Over the Rainbow" is a famous song from the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, about a magic place far away.

paragraphs.context: “Welcome back,” came a soft, lovely voice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: When they open their eyes, Morgan is there. They hug her.

paragraphs.context: “Once upon a time, there was a boy who wasted time,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells a story about a boy. The watch teaches him that time is very important and he must use it well.

paragraphs.context: “Sometimes the boy was afraid to stand up for himself,”
paragraphs.simple: The feather teaches the boy that a small creature can be very brave.

paragraphs.context: “Sometimes the boy did not respect nature,”
paragraphs.simple: The lotus flower teaches the boy that nature is full of wonderful things.

paragraphs.context: “Sometimes the boy didn’t want to study other times and places,”
paragraphs.simple: The bark painting teaches him that the old ways of ancient peoples have mystery, magic and wisdom.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you,” she said, “for helping this boy learn his lessons.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan thanks them for breaking the spell.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan thanks them for helping the boy learn and for ending the spell. Jack still asks: "What boy?"

paragraphs.context: Then something magical happened.
paragraphs.simple: Very quickly, as if in a magic wind, Teddy changed. He was not a dog any more. He was a boy!
paragraphs.tone: The big surprise of the series.

paragraphs.context: “Meet my young helper from Camelot,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy is a boy from Camelot.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the boy is her young helper from Camelot.

background.note: Camelot is King Arthur's castle and town in the old British stories. Morgan's library is there.

paragraphs.context: The boy glanced up.
paragraphs.simple: The boy had a friendly face with small brown spots, and happy eyes. His hair was the colour of Teddy's fur. He was about ten.

paragraphs.context: “And I hope next time you’ll ask before trying the spells in my spell book,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the boy became a dog.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan wants him to ask before he uses her magic book. The boy smiled in a shy way: he turned himself into a dog by mistake.

paragraphs.context: “If you like, you can keep calling me Teddy,” the boy said.
paragraphs.simple: They can still call him Teddy, or Ted.

paragraphs.context: “Ted is training to work in my library at Camelot,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ted is learning to be a librarian.
paragraphs.simple: Ted is learning to work in Morgan's library. He is very good at magic.

paragraphs.context: “The story of the Titanic, the story of White Buffalo Woman
paragraphs.simple: Ted will write down the four stories from their trips for Morgan's library.

background.note: White Buffalo Woman is a holy woman in Lakota stories. Jack and Annie heard her story in book 18.

paragraphs.context: Jack pulled on his pack. With a heavy heart, he followed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was very sad as he went down the ladder.

paragraphs.context: Morgan and Ted were at the window.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan and Ted seemed to shine in the evening light. Morgan says the tree house will come back.

paragraphs.context: He felt dazed as they walked silently through the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was too surprised to think. They walked home quietly as the sun went down.

paragraphs.context: “Like living in Dreamtime,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot find the right words. Annie says it was like living in Dreamtime, a magic time. Jack agrees.

paragraphs.context: Australia is the world’s smallest and flattest continent.
paragraphs.simple: Australia is the smallest and flattest continent. It is the only country that is a whole continent.

background.note: 3 million square miles is about 7.7 million square kilometres.

paragraphs.context: At one time, all the continents on earth were part of one huge land mass.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago all land was one piece. Australia moved away about 200 million years ago, so its animals changed in their own way.

paragraphs.context: Among the animals that live on Australia are 170 different kinds of marsupials
paragraphs.simple: Australia has 170 kinds of marsupials. Outside Australia, only opossums are marsupials.

background.note: Opossums live in North and South America. In this list they are the only marsupials outside Australia.

paragraphs.context: Kangaroos have been in Australia for 25 million years.
paragraphs.simple: There are ten kangaroos for every person in Australia. They hop at about 18 kilometres an hour, and for short times up to about 48.

background.note: "mph" means miles per hour. 11 mph is about 18 kilometres an hour.

paragraphs.context: Koalas feed on gum trees
paragraphs.simple: Gum trees are also called eucalyptus trees. Their oil is used in medicine for colds.

background.note: Eucalyptus oil has a strong, fresh smell. It is used in sweets and in medicines for colds.

paragraphs.context: In Aborigine myth, the Rainbow Serpent not only brings rain
paragraphs.simple: The Aborigines are the first people of Australia. In one of their old stories, a giant snake called the Rainbow Serpent brings rain and helped make the world.

paragraphs.context: At the beginning of time, the Rainbow Serpent awoke from sleep
paragraphs.simple: At the start of time, the Serpent woke up and came up through the ground. It moved over the empty land and left deep lines behind it.

paragraphs.context: The Rainbow Serpent called to the frogs to come out
paragraphs.mainIdea: How rivers and lakes were made.
paragraphs.simple: The Serpent tickled the frogs, and they laughed. Water came out of their mouths and filled the Serpent's tracks. That made rivers and lakes.

paragraphs.context: Grass grew. Then all creatures
paragraphs.simple: Then grass grew, and all the animals woke up and took their places on the earth.

a bit.example: He looked a bit older than Jack

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as if.example: They looked as if they were dancing.

as soon as.meaning: At the moment when; right after.
as soon as.example: as soon as I get home

at first.example: The sound was very faint at first.

at least.meaning: You say "at least" to talk about the one good thing in a bad situation.
at least.example: But at least I got to have exciting adventures

at top speed.example: The emus raced by at top speed.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: they are about to set out

break the silence.meaning: To make the first sound after a time of quiet.

break the spell.example: Thank you for breaking the spell.

burst into flames.meaning: To suddenly start to burn strongly.
burst into flames.example: a tree suddenly burst into flames

by a mile.meaning: By a very large amount. "She can out-hop you by a mile" means she can hop much, much better than you.
by a mile.example: She can out-hop you by a mile.

by heart.meaning: If you know something by heart, you can say it from memory, without looking.
by heart.example: He knew the note by heart now.

catch up.meaning: To come up to someone who is in front of you, by going faster.

change into.meaning: To make someone or something become a different thing.
change into.example: I accidentally changed myself into a dog

come over.meaning: When a feeling comes over you, you suddenly start to feel it.
come over.example: A feeling of dread came over Jack.

cut down.meaning: To cut a tree so that it falls to the ground.

dash off.meaning: To leave or run away very fast.
dash off.example: Annie had dashed off in the other direction.

feed on.meaning: To eat something as your usual food.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.

find your voice.meaning: To be able to speak again after a shock or surprise.

get out of here.example: We have to get out of here.

go back to sleep.meaning: To start sleeping again after waking up.

good luck.meaning: You say "Good luck!" to wish someone well.

hand to hand.meaning: Holding hands, one person to the next. (A chapter title.)

hands and knees.meaning: "On his hands and knees" means on the ground, with his hands and knees touching it, like a dog.

have no choice.meaning: To have only one thing that you can do.

help out.meaning: To help someone, especially when they have a problem.
help out.example: Once again, Teddy helped us out

hold out.meaning: To put your hand or arm out toward someone.
hold out.example: She held out her free hand to Jack.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, because you are waiting or afraid.
hold your breath.example: as if they all were holding their breath

i'm afraid.meaning: "I'm afraid" here means "I am sorry to say". It is a polite way to tell bad news.

in case.meaning: Because something might happen. "In case he needed to" means because he might need to.
in case.example: in case he needed to look something up

in search of.example: in search of their last gift

in shock.meaning: Very surprised and upset, so that you cannot think clearly.

instead of.meaning: In the place of something else.
instead of.example: on his chest instead of on his back

keep an eye on.meaning: To watch someone or something carefully.
keep an eye on.example: Jack kept his eye on Annie

keep going.meaning: To not stop; to go on.
keep going.example: He held it up with his arms and kept going.

late for.meaning: Coming after the time you should come. "Don't be late for dinner" means come home before dinner starts.

look out.meaning: To look through a window or opening to the outside.

look up.meaning: 1. To look up a word or fact is to find it in a book. 2. To look up is to raise your eyes.

lost at sea.meaning: A ship "lost at sea" sank in the sea and was never found again.
lost at sea.example: A gift from a ship lost at sea,

make sense.meaning: To be easy to understand; to seem right. "That doesn't make sense" means "I don't understand. That can't be right."

no longer.example: He was no longer a dog.

not at all.meaning: Not in any way. "Not a bear at all" means it is really not a bear.

oh brother.meaning: "Oh, brother!" is something you say when you feel a little silly or tired of something.

once again.example: Once again, Jack and Annie followed him.

once upon a time.meaning: The way many old stories begin. It means "A long time ago".
once upon a time.example: “Once upon a time, there was a boy who wasted time,”

or so.meaning: About; more or less. "About ten or so" means about ten years old.

or what.meaning: You add "or what?" to a question when you do not understand what is happening and want an answer.
or what.example: Are they making a bonfire now or what?

over the rainbow.meaning: "Over the rainbow" means far away, in a magic place. It comes from a famous song.

put on.meaning: "Put on bursts of speed" means suddenly go much faster for a short time.
put on.example: can put on bursts of speed

put one's hand out.meaning: To hold your hand out away from your body, to reach or touch something.
put one's hand out.example: Then he put his other hand out and touched the wall.

put out.meaning: To put out a fire is to stop it burning.
put out.example: The heavy rain was putting out the wildfire.

put something on.meaning: To put clothes or a bag on your body so that you wear it.

rainbow serpent.meaning: In the stories of the Aborigines, the Rainbow Serpent is a great magic snake that gives life and brings rain.
rainbow serpent.example: In Dreamtime, there is a Rainbow Serpent

school bus.meaning: A bus that takes children to and from school.

set out.example: Now they are about to set out in search of their last gift

speaking of.meaning: You say "Speaking of ..." when you want to talk more about something that was just said.

stand up for yourself.meaning: To say or do what is right for you, and not let others be unkind to you.

take off.meaning: To leave or run away suddenly and fast.
take off.example: She took off after the dogs.

take place.example: Their myths take place in a time they call “Dreamtime.”

teddy bear.meaning: A soft toy bear. Annie says the koala looks like a "live" (real, living) teddy bear.

time to go.meaning: "Time to go" means "We must leave now."

too bad.meaning: "That's too bad" means "That is a pity" or "That is sad."

turn into.meaning: To change and become something different.
turn into.example: had turned into a big black cloud

turn over.meaning: To move so that the other side is on top.

under a spell.meaning: Controlled by magic, so that you cannot be or do what you usually are or do.
under a spell.example: This little dog is under a spell

wake up.meaning: To stop sleeping, or to make someone stop sleeping.
wake up.example: We didn’t mean to wake you up.

welcome back.meaning: What you say to someone who comes back after being away.
welcome back.example: “Welcome back,” came a soft, lovely voice.

what'd i tell you.meaning: "What'd I tell you?" means "I told you so! I was right."

with a heavy heart.example: With a heavy heart, he followed.

write down.meaning: To write something on paper so that you do not forget it.

you're kidding.meaning: "You're kidding!" means "That can't be true!" or "Are you joking?"

you're welcome.meaning: What you say when someone thanks you.

oh man.meaning: Something you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. "Oh, man!" is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a real man.
